To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
PEG-coating of oxidized polystyrene significantly reduces fibrinogen adsorbed, and that branched and linear forms of PEG are equally effective.

(1) branched and linear polyethylene glycols (PEGs) of 1500-20,000 MW were covalently coupled to polystyrene by using poly(ethylene imide) as a spacer; and (2) the adsorption of fibrinogen to these surfaces was reduced by a factor of 5-20 relative to uncoated polystyrenes.
PEG-derivatized PS surfaces have been developed that are resistant to fibrinogen adsorbtion, and that the ELISA technique is useful for estimating protein adsorption levels.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a simple, inexpensive method for the preparation of PEG-coated polymer surfaces.
developing chemistry for the preparation of PEG-coated surfaces and with the ability of PEG-coating to reject proteins from surfaces.
developing chemistry to provide covalent attachment of PEG on polycarbonate and poly(ethylene imide) surfaces.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of PEG-coated surfaces is an effective means of reducing protein adsorption.
PEG coatings on PS can reduce fibrinogen adsorbed to levels that are significantly lower than those found on uncoated PS.
the PEG-epoxidation chemistry is a simple and effective method for producing PEG-coated surfaces, and that these surfaces are highly effective in rejecting fibrinogen adsorbed onto the surfaces.

PEGs of various molecular weights and architectures can be covalently attached to PS surfaces, that these PEG-coated surfaces can be used to reduce fibrinogen adsorbtion, and that ELISA can be used to measure protein adsorption.
the PEG coating chemistry developed here is a robust method for preparing surfaces that resist protein adsorption.
the use of a PEG-coated surface to reduce protein adsorption and subsequent cell adhesion can be readily achieved on a variety of substrates.

the PEG-epoxy coupling chemistry can be readily applied to a variety of surfaces and that the ELISA technique is an effective means for estimating protein adsorption.
